Beyond 4 Bits: Data-Centric Post-Training
Quantization and Recovery

Rhea Sanjay Sukthanker Email: rsukthanker@microsoft.comriccardo.grazzi.4@gmail.com    Riccardo Grazzi Affiliation: Applied Sciences Group (ASG), Microsoft  Microsoft Research Email: jameshensman@microsoft.compcameron@microsoft.com    James Hensman Affiliation: Applied Sciences Group (ASG), Microsoft  Microsoft Research    Pashmina Cameron
Abstract

Post-training quantization (PTQ) compresses the weights of a trained model with limited compute and data. Down to 4 bits it is near-lossless, but at 2 bits scalar PTQ configurations fall to chance-level accuracy. We study three choices usually treated as implementation details that matter little at 4 bits but decide 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data, and the recovery fine-tuning data, across six dense and mixture-of experts models (ranging from 3.83.8 to 3232B parameters). Representation is the largest factor and vector codebooks restore usable models where scalar PTQ pipelines collapse. Most of the remaining loss in accuracy is on generative tasks, and the amount of performance drop is model-dependent. Furthermore, at a short recovery budget, calibration and recovery data are coupled. The best recovery data depends on the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly. The resulting recipe involves a vector codebook representation, a small task-aligned calibration mixture, and an inexpensive codebook-only recovery stage. Including codebooks, it uses about 2.32.3 effective bits per weight and retains 8989 to 97%97\% of full-precision question-answering (QA) accuracy where scalar PTQ is at chance, and, including recovery, uses 1.41.4 to 30×30\times less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline.

1 Introduction

Post-training quantization (PTQ) is standard for serving large language models under tight memory budgets. At 4 bits (W4A16: 4-bit weights, 16-bit activations), it costs only a few accuracy points (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Ashkboos et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025b). At 2 bits, scalar PTQ falls to chance-level accuracy (Egiazarian et al., 2024; Chee et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024a; Figure 1a), and quantized reasoning models can overthink and loop (Lotfi et al., 2026). Richer codebooks (Van Baalen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Egiazarian et al., 2024; Tseng et al., 2024a) or learned quantization (Liu et al., 2024b; Du et al., 2024; Dadgarnia et al., 2026) trade compute for quality, yet 2-bit models still lag their 4-bit counterparts.

Three choices usually treated as implementation details govern 2-bit quality: the quantization representation, the calibration data that shape quantization, and the recovery data used to fine-tune the quantized model. They matter little at 4 bits but become consequential below 4 bits, where calibration and recovery data also interact, so tuning them separately can be misleading. We study 2-bit quantization and recovery across six dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) models (3.83.8 to 3232B parameters) and propose an actionable recipe (Section 5) for low-budget 2-bit quantization. Our primary observations are:

  • •

    Representation dominates at 2 bits. Every scalar PTQ pipeline we test falls to random chance-level, while vector PTQ at ∼2.3{\sim}2.3 effective bits keeps 8989–97%97\% of a full-precision model’s question-answering accuracy without training, using 3939–304×304\times less compute than trained scalar methods (Table 4).

  • •

    Loss of reasoning ability is model-dependent. Question-answering retention is similar across models, but HumanEval (codegen) retention spans 45%45\% (Phi-4-mini, Qwen3-8B) to 81%81\% (Qwen3-MoE), tracking the model and its scale more than the quantizer (Figure 4).

  • •

    Calibration and recovery data interact. Choosing them jointly improves Phi-4-mini’s accuracy on generation tasks from 11.1%11.1\% (web calibration) to 45.7%45.7\% (math calibration, web recovery); the best recovery data flips with calibration on all three dense models we study (Tables 1 and 2).

The proposed recipe is a vector representation with a task-aligned calibration mixture and a short codebook-only recovery stage. With recovery, it narrows the gap to 4-bit models while using 1.41.4 to 30×30\times less compute than the strongest quantization-aware-training (QAT) baseline; a cheap per-model check handles model dependence (Section 5). Upon acceptance, we will release our code, Hessian mixtures, and quantized models.

2 Related Work

Scalar PTQ. GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023) sets the near-lossless 4-bit weight-only baseline via approximate second-order error minimization; AWQ (Lin et al., 2024) and SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023) rescale salient channels, while QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) and SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2025b) rotate weights before rounding. The scalar PTQ configurations we evaluate collapse at 2 bits without any further quantization-aware training or recovery (Section 4.4).

Vector and ultra-low-bit quantization. Codebooks give better rate-distortion below 3 bits. QuIP (Chee et al., 2023) adds incoherence processing to adaptive scalar rounding; QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024a) pairs it with lattice codebooks and fine-tuning. AQLM, GPTVQ, VPTQ, and QTIP (Egiazarian et al., 2024; Van Baalen et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024a; Tseng et al., 2024b) use additive, hierarchical, or trellis-coded codebooks. YAQA (Tseng et al., 2026) adds a Fisher-weighted rounding objective. Non-uniform (Kim et al., 2024) and 1-bit (Huang et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2024b) methods also target lower precision to go even beyond 2-bits.

Trained scalar quantization. OmniQuant (Shao et al., 2024) learns clipping thresholds block-wise, and GSQ (Dadgarnia et al., 2026) learns scalar-grid assignments through a Gumbel-Softmax relaxation; we use GSQ as an intermediate-cost scalar baseline between PTQ and QAT.

Calibration data. PTQ usually calibrates on a few hundred C4 or WikiText-2 sequences (Frantar et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024; Shao et al., 2024; Egiazarian et al., 2024). Calibration data affect 4-bit models (Williams and Aletras, 2024) and pruning (Bandari et al., 2024; Ji et al., 2025), and self-generated text can replace curated corpora (Williams et al., 2025). We find that calibration data effects 2-bit PTQ methods much more than on 4-bit methods and this effect is consistent across representations and recipe grids (Appendix A.6).

Evaluating quantized LLMs. Quantization costs generation, reasoning, and knowledge-intensive tasks more than perplexity or multiple-choice QA as suggested by (Jaiswal et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Jin et al., 2024; Kurtic et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a), and robustness depends on model size and token density (Dettmers and Zettlemoyer, 2023; Kumar et al., 2025; Ouyang et al., 2025). We confirm this gap at 2 bits and show that the degradation of generation quality depends on calibration, recovery data and model-scale.

Recovery for quantized models. Distillation-based recovery (Hinton et al., 2015) narrows the quantization gap without full QAT. LLM-QAT and BitDistiller (Liu et al., 2024b; Du et al., 2024) retrain all weights; LoRA and QLoRA (Hu et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023) add high-precision parameters; closest to ours, EfficientQAT (Chen et al., 2025) trains all weights block-wise, then quantization parameters end to end; ParetoQ (Liu et al., 2026) studies extremely low-bit QAT. AQLM and QuIP# fine-tune codebooks or continuous parameters after quantization. PV-Tuning (Malinovskii et al., 2024) additionally also learns discrete assignments to the codebook vectors. In this work we use codebook-only recovery and show that its best data flips with the calibration data, so the two must be chosen jointly (Section 4.2).

3 Background and Method

We study post-training quantization followed by recovery fine-tuning at the same format and bitwidth.

3.1 Scalar and Vector Quantization

Scalar quantization maps each weight to one of 2b2^{b} levels, x^=s⁡(q−z)\hat{x}=s(q-z), with integer code qq, per-group scale ss, and optional zero-point zz. Error-aware PTQ, such as GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023), minimizes output error on a calibration distribution XX with input Hessian HX=𝔼x∼X​[x​x⊤]H_{X}=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim X}[xx^{\top}]:

minW^∈𝒬⁡𝔼x∼X​‖(W−W^)​x‖22=minW^∈𝒬⁡Tr⁡[(W−W^)​HX​(W−W^)⊤],\min_{\hat{W}\in\mathcal{Q}}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim X}\!\big\|(W-\hat{W})x\big\|_{2}^{2}=\min_{\hat{W}\in\mathcal{Q}}\operatorname{Tr}\!\big[(W-\hat{W})H_{X}(W-\hat{W})^{\top}\big], (1)

where 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is the set of representable weights. Vector quantization maps each dd-dimensional sub-vector wiw_{i} to an entry of a learned codebook 𝒞={ck}k=1K\mathcal{C}=\{c_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, w^i=cai\hat{w}_{i}=c_{a_{i}}, using weight correlations that scalar grids miss. VPTQ (Liu et al., 2024a) solves Equation 1 over codebooks. Structured-curvature methods such as KronQ (Lee et al., 2026) and YAQA (Tseng et al., 2026) use Kronecker-factored full-model KL curvature and YAQA rounds onto trellis-coded sets.

Calibration mixtures. The objective depends on the data only through HXH_{X}. A mixture with weights αj≥0\alpha_{j}\geq 0, ∑jαj=1\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}=1, over domains with Hessians HjH_{j} has H𝜶=∑jαj​HjH_{\bm{\alpha}}=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}H_{j} would allow one to approximate the hessian for different data distributions, cheaply. We sweep mixtures by reweighting precomputed Hessians without re-collecting hessians on actual dataset mixtures; each mixture still needs its own quantization pass. For YAQA we mix the Kronecker input and output factors separately, approximating re-estimation on different dataset mixtures.

3.2 Recovery Fine-Tuning

Recovery freezes the quantized backbone and trains only quantization parameters: the codebook 𝒞\mathcal{C} with assignments fixed, or the scales ss (and zz). QAT backpropagates through the quantizer with a straight-through estimator (Liu et al., 2024b) and keeps optimizer state for all weights (≈ 14​P{\approx}\,14P bytes for PP parameters). Recovery keeps the bitwidth and needs only a teacher and student (≈ 2​P+b​P/8{\approx}\,2P+bP/8 bytes. We distill from the full-precision model with ℒ=αℒCE+(1−α)τ2KL(σ(zt/τ)∥σ(zs/τ))\mathcal{L}=\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+(1-\alpha)\,\tau^{2}\operatorname{KL}\big(\sigma(z_{t}/\tau)\,\|\,\sigma(z_{s}/\tau)\big), where ztz_{t} and zsz_{s} are teacher and student logits, σ\sigma is the softmax, τ\tau the temperature, and α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 unless noted. Our recovery pipeline involves codebook-only recovery. In the appendix we cover alternative losses and logit truncation (Appendix A.7), a scale-only recovery scalar control (Appendix A.7), and finetuning with low-rank adapters (Hu et al., 2022; Dettmers et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024b), which add half-precision parameters (Appendix A.11).

4 Experiments and Results

4.1 Experimental setup

Models and quantizers. We evaluate Phi-4-mini (Abouelenin et al., 2025) (3.8B, instruct), Llama-3.1-8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) (base), and Qwen3-30B-A3B (Yang et al., 2025) (reasoning MoE, ∼3{\sim}3B active). Qwen3-8B (reasoning) checks the calibration and recovery choices; OLMoE-1B-7B (Muennighoff et al., 2025) (instruct MoE) and Qwen3-32B (reasoning, dense) extend the comparisons to smaller MoEs and large-scale dense models, respectively. The scalar baselines we use are SpinQuant (Liu et al., 2025b) and QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) at group size 128. Furthermore, we observe that learned rotations do not help at 2 bits (Appendix A.3). The vector-quantization baselines we study are VPTQ (Liu et al., 2024a) (2162^{16}-entry codebook over 8-dimensional vectors) and YAQA (Tseng et al., 2026), a Fisher-weighted trellis quantizer, both in the same incoherence-rotated frame; we report native (unrotated) VPTQ where it is stronger. We also compare vector quantization against GSQ (Dadgarnia et al., 2026) (scalar PTQ with learned assignments) and BitDistiller (Du et al., 2024) (scalar QAT). In our experiments we quantize attention and MLP projections, including every MoE expert. Routers, embeddings, norms and the language modeling head stay in half precision. Our ablation on the router precision in Appendix A.10, suggests that the router is pretty robust to quantization. Counting indices, codebooks, and scales, every method uses 2.092.09–2.332.33 effective bits per weight. In the MoEs, VPTQ shares codebooks across experts, while YAQA operates with a single large codebook for all weights. We evaluate dequantized weights, report packed-size storage estimates, and count dominant model passes, amortizing Hessian collection over the calibration sweep. Configurations and protocols are in Appendices A.3, A.2.

Calibration and evaluation. For calibration data we primarily focus on web, instruction, math (OpenR1-Math), code, and their mixtures. We report an AvgQA metric which averages over seven QA tasks: MMLU (5-shot) (Hendrycks et al., 2020), WinoGrande (Sakaguchi et al., 2021), and LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016), scored by accuracy, and ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge (Clark et al., 2018), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), scored by length-normalized accuracy (all 0-shot except MMLU). We report an AvgGen metric which averages GSM8K (5-shot, strict match) (Cobbe et al., 2021) and HumanEval (0-shot, pass@1) (Chen et al., 2021); we also report IFEval (0-shot, prompt-strict) (Zhou et al., 2023). Results use bfloat16 evaluation (P-bf16) unless a table is marked P-fp16 (float16); the two differ only marginally in our analyses.

4.2 Calibration and recovery data are not separable

The best recovery data depends on the calibration data. We quantize Phi-4-mini and Llama-3.1-8B with web or math calibration data, then apply short codebook-only recovery (3,2003{,}200 examples) on web or math data (Figure 2, Table 1). Math recovery helps the web-calibrated base but not the math-calibrated one, giving a negative interaction on both models with 95%95\% intervals excluding zero (Table 2). Calibration is the larger factor and math calibration raises generation under either recovery source. Furthermore, whether to recover or not is model-dependent. Every recovery stage helps the instruction-tuned Phi-4-mini. However for the pretrained base Llama-3.1-8B, math calibration and no recovery procedure works best. The interaction sign also holds on a logit scale and these results cover one domain pair at a short budget (Table 8).

Prospective confirmation. Before collecting Qwen3-8B data, we pre-registered its 2×22\times 2 design, analysis, and three predictions (Appendix A.9): a negative interaction, web recovery at least as good as math recovery on the math-calibrated base, and a larger interaction on HumanEval than on GSM8K. All of these predictions hold (Table 2) on this model. The interaction also stays negative on held-out tasks, with fresh Phi-4-mini calibration samples, and with disjoint recovery-data samples (Figure 3; Appendices A.9 and Table 25). On prompt-independent tasks alone (MBPP, MATH-500), the interaction effect is clear only on Phi-4-mini (Appendix A.9).

What the interaction does not imply. It is not a rule to “add the domain absent from calibration”: on Phi-4-mini every short recovery improves over its base, and calibration changes only which recovery source helps more.

4.3 Scalar PTQ collapses in the tested pipelines

Scalar PTQ has a sharp 2-bit cliff. At 4 bits the best scalar method stays close to bf16; at 2 bits every tested scalar pipeline falls to the random QA floor with 0.0 accuracy on generation, on all three models (Table 3 and curves in Appendix A.15).

Vector codebooks revive 2-bit models. Vector pipelines raise 2-bit QA into the mid-60s from the 20s floor on all three families, and YAQA stays ahead in a matched-bit control (Table 13).

4.4 Comparisons with trained scalar quantization

On question answering, the vector pipelines match or beat GSQ and BitDistiller on every model; on generation, YAQA beats both (Table 4). Within our recipe grid and bit budget, YAQA leads on every model. GSQ collapses to the random-accuracy floor on the MoEs.

4.5 Calibration chiefly controls generation

With the quantizer fixed, calibration data mainly moves generation: across recipes, AvgGen varies by 13.513.5–26.726.7 points per model, while AvgQA varies by only 3.93.9–7.57.5 (Table 5). At 4 bits, the same sweep moves scalar models by at most 1.61.6 QA and 7.97.9 generation points (Table 17). Math calibration gives the best generation on the dense models, a targeted mixture on Qwen3-MoE, and broad web-heavy data the best QA.

Generation retention is model-dependent. QA retention is similar across models, but HumanEval retention ranges from under half to over 80%80\% (Figure 4). Within Qwen3 the dense 32B model retains far more generation than the dense 8B one, so model scale is necessary for strong retention. Furthermore, the precision of the MoE router barely changes accuracy (Appendix A.10).

4.6 Codebook-only recovery is model-dependent

Table 8 pairs each 2-bit base with long codebook-only recovery on the same recipe data. On Phi-4-mini, recovery changes QA little but roughly doubles HumanEval. On Qwen3-MoE it changes both little; on Llama-3.1-8B base model, QA decreases in all three long runs and generation has no consistent gain. IFEval falls on most Phi-4-mini recipes under completion prompts and is mostly, but not uniformly, preserved under the chat template (Appendix Table  35). Furthermore recovery does not help 2-bit models which hit the random floor. Scale-only recovery on a collapsed scalar 2-bit model leaves it near the floor (Appendix A.7).

Under the deployment prompt, short recovery need not cost instruction following. With the chat template, web recovery of the math-calibrated Phi-4-mini base raises GSM8K from 55.055.0 to 58.958.9, HumanEval from 34.134.1 to 43.943.9, and IFEval from 40.340.3 to 44.544.5 (four recovery seeds); math recovery raises GSM8K further (61.561.5) but lowers IFEval to 37.937.9 (Table 36). The best recovery data still flips with calibration and math recovery gives the highest AvgGen from the web base and web recovery from the math base.

Recovery data matter more than distillation hyperparameters. The type of knowledge distillation loss, the teacher precision, temperature, and top-kk truncation change AvgQA little. A 4-bit teacher matches a bf16 one, and dropping the teacher keeps most generation gain (Appendix A.7). With fixed web recovery data, generation gains 6.36.3 points by 3,2003{,}200 examples and then plateaus, while QA rises slowly with more data (Figure 5). Recovery with low-rank-adaptor is in Appendix A.11.

4.7 Overthinking under quantization

We reproduce the overthinking failure mode of Lotfi et al. (2026) on Qwen3-30B-A3B, a reasoning model with an explicit thinking mode at 2-bits. On MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021) levels 4–5 with greedy decoding, we compare the bf16 ceiling with the best 4-bit checkpoint and the expert-shared 2-bit VPTQ web/mixed 0.7/0.30.7/0.3 checkpoint of Table 10 in the Appendix. Accuracy is exact match on the final answer. “Markers/1k” counts hesitation and branch-forking tokens (e.g., “Wait”, “But”, “Alternatively”) per 1,0001{,}000 generated tokens. The loop score is the repeated 44-gram fraction. Table 6 shows that 2-bit quantization amplifies overthinking without collapse. Accuracy falls (0.675→0.450.675\to 0.45), and the hesitation-marker rate, loop score, and length-cap hit rate rise. A small repetition penalty reduces looping and improves 2-bit accuracy (Table 7). Figure 15 in the appendix shows the effect of a repetition penalty.

5 A Practical Recipe for Accurate 2-Bit Models

Table 9 and the highlighted box below give the recipe. The representation default holds across six models, including two MoEs; the calibration defaults come from the three primary model families. Whether and how to recover depends on the model and the calibration data, so the recipe adds a cheap per-model check. Screening kk calibrated bases costs kk quantization passes, 2​k2k short recoveries (≈100{\approx}100 PFLOP each for a 4B-parameter model and 3​k3k evaluations, far less than QAT.

6 Conclusion and Future work

Conclusion

At 2 bits, quality depends heavily on representation, calibration data, and recovery. A vector codebook restores most collapsed accuracy and a task-aligned calibration mixture and short codebook-only recovery stage narrow the generation gap at much less compute than QAT. The data choices are not separable at a short recovery budget: calibration domain drives generation, and the best recovery data depends on it. Across three models and a held-out composite, math recovery helps a web-calibrated base but not a math-calibrated one (clearest on Phi-4-mini). Tuning the two data choices separately can therefore select the wrong recovery data, and whether to recover must be validated per model. Most remaining loss is in generation, whose measurement depends on prompt format and numerical precision.

Limitations and Future Work.

We measure base and data-sample variability only on Phi-4-mini, and replicate bases share one rotation and one recovery seed. The interaction covers one domain pair and one quantizer (YAQA) at a short budget; we did not re-run the 2×22\times 2 design at long budgets. We leave these studies for future work.

Use of AI Tools

All ideas presented in this paper are original to the authors or built upon the related work cited herein. AI-based tools were used only in an assistive capacity: to sharpen the clarity of the authors’ initial drafts, to prepare initial drafts, to help typeset the paper in LaTeX, to rephrase sections, to improve the presentation of figures and tables, to correct grammatical errors and make sentences more salient, and to act as a coding assistant that implements the authors’ ideas. All technical content, claims, and conclusions were conceived, verified, and approved by the authors.

Acknowledgments

We are deeply grateful to Hari VK and Andrey Rybalchenko (Microsoft Research, Cambridge) for their extensive work to make application of incoherence rotations automatic and robust. This work allowed us to reliably test the effect of incoherent rotations on a large number of dense and mixture-of-experts transformer models with different architectures. The work underpins our rotated scalar baselines and the incoherence-rotated frame in which our vector quantizers operate on the MoE models, and it was essential for extending this study from dense models to Qwen3-30B-A3B and OLMoE-1B-7B.

Appendix A Additional Experimental Details and Results

In this section we provide additional details about out pipeline, evaluations and ablation studies on different knobs of the 2-bit quantization pipeline.

A.1 Evaluation protocols and result provenance

Our results use four protocols. All of them run with lm-evaluation-harness 0.4.120.4.12, transformers 4.53.34.53.3, and greedy decoding. They use 5-shot MMLU and GSM8K (strict match) and 0-shot HumanEval (pass@1) and IFEval (prompt-strict). Most controlled comparisons use one protocol. Table 4 mixes labeled native-VPTQ P-bf16 entries into a P-fp16 comparison.

P-fp16

(completion prompts, float16) covers the main sweeps in Tables 3, 4, and 5. It also covers the Qwen3-MoE row of Table 8, the calibration sweeps, the recovery budget curve, and the Core6 seed table.

P-fp32

repeats P-fp16 in float32 for the two Phi-4-mini checkpoints affected by float16 decoding (Appendix A.8).

P-bf16

is the canonical controlled protocol. It uses completion prompts, bfloat16, per-item logs, and a finite-logit probe. It covers the Phi-4-mini and Llama-3.1-8B 2×22\times 2 design (Figure 2 and Table 21) and the Phi-4-mini and Llama-3.1-8B rows of Table 8. It also covers teacher-free recovery, learned SpinQuant, calibration-side controls, and the dense-32B and OLMoE evaluations.

P-chat

covers chat-template tables. It uses each model’s chat template with thinking disabled and at most 1,0241{,}024 generated tokens. It runs in bfloat16 unless marked.

A.2 evaluation details

Evaluation and reproducibility.

We score tasks with an lm-evaluation-harness-based split-task orchestrator (Gao et al., 2021). Multiple-choice tasks use log-likelihood scoring. MMLU and GSM8K use 55-shot prompting. GSM8K and HumanEval use greedy decoding with temperature 00 and no sampling. They are scored by strict match and pass@1. Compute accounting uses 128128 scalar-calibration sequences and 128128–2,0482{,}048 vector-Hessian sequences per domain. Seed 4242 is the default.

A.3 Per-method quantization configurations

Table 11 summarizes the quantization and recovery settings. Unless noted, methods target 2-bit weights at group size 128128 and use the protocol of §A.2 with seed 4242.

QuaRot and SpinQuant (scalar PTQ).

QuaRot and SpinQuant apply an incoherence rotation before scale-only ≈2.12\approx\!2.12-bit GPTQ quantization (Appendix A.2). QuaRot uses a fixed randomized Hadamard transform with activation ordering, Hessian-ordered columns, error feedback, and damping 0.10.1. SpinQuant uses residual-stream and per-head rotations (R1R_{1}, R2R_{2}) at randomized-Hadamard initialization, with experts rotated separately on Qwen3-MoE. Both methods consume 128128 calibration sequences and add no trained weights.

Learned-rotation in Spinquant.

We test learned SpinQuant rotations on the two dense primary models (Table 12). We optimize R1R_{1} and R2R_{2} with Cayley SGD for 100100 steps on the same 128128 calibration sequences from each domain. We use learning rates 1.51.5 and 0.250.25, then the same GPTQ quantization. Learned rotations leave all 2-bit models at the random-accuracy floor and barely change best-domain 4-bit AvgQA (Table 12). The scalar cliff is not from the unoptimized rotation. We could not fit the full-precision copy needed for Qwen3-30B-A3B, so its SpinQuant entries keep the Hadamard initialization.

VPTQ (vector PTQ).

VPTQ maps each 88-dimensional weight sub-vector to one of 65,53665{,}536 (2162^{16}) codebook entries (2.002.00 index bits). Dense models use one 11 MiB fp16 codebook per linear layer (2.122.12–2.332.33 effective bits). MoEs use expert-shared codebooks (2.092.09–2.142.14). VPTQ uses channel-independent second-order optimization over a shared Hadamard frame with input Hessians collected by calibration domain. The rate control of §A.4 uses one model-wide 262,144262{,}144-entry (2182^{18}) codebook, giving 2.252.25 index bits and 2.262.26 effective bits.

YAQA (vector PTQ).

YAQA uses a trellis codebook with Fisher-weighted, Kronecker-factored curvature from the full-model KL objective and 2.252.25 index bits. Sign vectors and a shared lookup table bring the rate to 2.262.26–2.312.31 effective bits. YAQA also retains a fine-tuning-ready codebook under the same incoherence rotation, with curvature estimated from 128128–2,0482{,}048 sequences per calibration domain.

GSQ (trained scalar).

GSQ learns discrete grid assignments through a Gumbel-softmax relaxation initialized with GPTQ (512512 sequences). It optimizes one transformer block at a time with detached inputs. It runs 1010 epochs over a 0.10.1B-token calibration set (48,82848{,}828 sequences of length 20482048) with group size 128128 and a Lion optimizer.

BitDistiller (full QAT).

BitDistiller trains a Hadamard-rotated 22-bit model with asymmetric activation clipping and CAKLD (β≈0.84\beta\approx 0.84). We run one FSDP full-shard epoch across 88 GPUs. We use sequence length 10241024, per-device batch 11, gradient accumulation 88 (effective batch 6464), learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} with cosine decay, and 10%10\% warmup. The recovery mixture has ∼500{\sim}500k dense-model sequences and ∼50{\sim}50k Qwen3-MoE sequences.

Codebook-only recovery (PTQ+RFT).

Recovery freezes the quantized backbone and discrete assignments, then updates only the continuous codebook, leaving the effective bitwidth unchanged. Scalar scale-only recovery is a limited control (Appendix A.7). We do not test zero-point recovery. This stage distills from a bf16 or a x4 times smaller 44-bit teacher. The objective optimized is a temperature-11 forward-KL loss plus next-token cross-entropy. We optimize it with AdamW at learning rate 10−410^{-4} and a cosine schedule. Long Phi-4-mini runs (Table 8 and the main run) use 88 GPUs, per-device batch 11, gradient accumulation 22, sequence length 4,0964{,}096 (65,53665{,}536 tokens per optimizer step), 5,5005{,}500 steps (≈360{\approx}360M tokens), and 550550 warmup steps on the recipe mixture. Llama uses the same layout for ≈185{\approx}185M tokens. Qwen3-MoE uses sequence length 512512, gradient accumulation 22, a device-sharded teacher, and ≈1.2{\approx}1.2M tokens. Controlled short runs cover the 2×22\times 2 design, budget curve, seeds, and teacher-free control. They run on one GPU with per-device batch 11, gradient accumulation 88, sequence length 1,0241{,}024 (88 sequences per step), and 4040 warmup steps. The 51,20051{,}200-example point keeps 88 sequences per step with 88-GPU data parallelism. Ablations and LoRA are in §A.7 and §A.11.

A.4 Per-domain vector-quantizer comparison

Table 14 compares VPTQ and YAQA by calibration domain. YAQA wins all completed dense-model comparisons. Expert-shared VPTQ stays close on Qwen3-MoE web, instruction, and code, and on Phi-4-mini math and code.

YAQA’s advantage is not a bit-rate advantage.

On Phi-4-mini, VPTQ trails YAQA even when it spends more bits. With per-linear (216,8)(2^{16},8) codebooks, VPTQ uses 2.332.33 effective bits and YAQA uses 2.272.27. At matched bits, a model-wide 2182^{18}-entry VPTQ codebook (2.262.26 bits) narrows but does not close the web gap and trails further on math (Table 13).

A.5 Cross-paradigm 2-bit comparison

Table 15 compares trained scalar checkpoints with the strongest in-budget vector PTQ result on the same model in AvgQA. The vector checkpoint leads across models. BitDistiller performs full-model QAT, GSQ performs layer-wise discrete optimization, and VPTQ and YAQA are PTQ without training the weights.

A.6 Complete cross-model calibration sweep

Table 16 keeps recipes evaluated on all three main model families. The final row summarizes the task-complete spread. The per-domain scalar sweep measures calibration sensitivity at 4 bits. Table 17 reports the AvgQA and AvgGen spread across web, instruction, math, code, and mixed domains, alongside the 2-bit YAQA spread (Tables 16 and 5). The 4-bit scalar spreads are smaller. The comparison crosses representations and recipe grids because 2-bit scalar models are at the random floor for every domain. It does not isolate a bitwidth-only effect (Table 17).

A.7 Codebook-only recovery ablations

The codebook-only ablation uses the Phi-4-mini 2-bit YAQA mw64 checkpoint with math+web calibration. The reference configuration is forward KL, τ=1\tau=1, full-vocabulary distillation, a bf16 teacher, and web recovery data. Each block varies one factor. Note that fixed-base reference differs from the web row of Table 8, which recovers the web-calibrated base.

Teacher-free recovery.

We recovered the math-calibrated Phi-4-mini base of Appendix A.8 on the same 3,2003{,}200 web examples with plain next-token cross-entropy and no teacher, keeping every other setting fixed (seed 4242, bfloat16 evaluation). It reaches the same qualitative level as forward-KL distillation from a 4-bit teacher (three seeds, Table 21) and stays above the no-recovery base. In this single-seed Phi-4-mini setting, the teacher improves the result, but recovery data accounts for most of the effect.

Scale-only recovery of a scalar 2-bit model.

We applied the same recovery recipe (forward KL, web data, 1,0241{,}024-token context) to a scalar 2-bit Phi-4-mini model. This setup uses Hadamard rotation, GPTQ with activation ordering, group size 128128, and scale-only recovery. We trained only the per-group scales, with the integer codes frozen (≈P/128{\approx}P/128 parameters). Recovery moves AvgQA only slightly off the floor, while GSM8K and HumanEval stay near zero. With fixed codes, rescaling does not rescue the scalar model. The same 3,2003{,}200-example web-recovery recipe helps 2-bit codebook models of Phi-4-mini (Tables 1 and 8). BitDistiller trains all weights and still trails no-recovery vector PTQ in generation (Figure 1b).

A.8 Controlled calibration–recovery interaction

To test additivity, we crossed web and math calibration bases with web and math recovery data on Phi-4-mini. All cells use codebook-only recovery with frozen assignments, 3,2003{,}200 examples, context length 1,0241{,}024, a 4-bit teacher, and seed 42. IFEval is held out from main-study AvgQA/AvgGen recipe selection. Core6 averages ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, PIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and LAMBADA and is not directly comparable to the paper’s seven-task AvgQA.

The recovery-data effect depends on the calibration base. Math recovery helps from the web base but not from the math base (Table 20; statistical summaries in Table 2). From the math base, math rather than web recovery trades higher GSM8K for lower HumanEval, Core6, and held-out IFEval (Table 20). Calibration and recovery data therefore cannot be tuned independently.

Quantity control.

Holding the web base, FineWeb-Edu recovery source, context length, and all optimization settings fixed, increasing recovery data from 800800 to 3,2003{,}200 examples leaves Core6 nearly unchanged and improves AvgGen. The complete budget curve uses the math-calibrated base (Table 22).

Data-source control.

At the same 3,2003{,}200-example budget, with every other recovery setting fixed, replacing filtered FineWeb-Edu with unfiltered C4 leaves Core6 and held-out IFEval essentially unchanged but lowers both generation tasks and AvgGen. The generation benefit is not explained by recovery-set size alone. FineWeb-Edu and C4 differ in filtering, distribution, and collection history, so this control identifies a data-source effect rather than isolating filtering quality. Over the tested range, quality and quantity both matter for recovery data. The calibration-side analogue follows.

Calibration-side controls.

We also varied the Hessian calibration set of the web-calibrated Phi-4-mini YAQA base (no recovery, bfloat16 evaluation, seven-task AvgQA). At a matched 256256 sequences, filtered FineWeb-Edu and unfiltered C4 Hessians give similar QA and only small generation differences. Growing the FineWeb-Edu set from 256256 to the 2,0482{,}048 sequences of our web base mainly improves QA while leaving AvgGen unchanged. The source effect is small and generation-side (the HumanEval gap is three problems), so we treat it only as initial experimental evidence.

Generalization to a second model family.

Repeating the 2×22\times 2 design on Llama-3.1-8B reproduces the same sign with smaller magnitude than Phi-4-mini. Filtered FineWeb-Edu recovery improves AvgGen while leaving Core6 essentially unchanged.

Recovery budget.

All cells use 3,200×1,024≈3.33{,}200\times 1{,}024\approx 3.3M recovery tokens. This is about 100100 PFLOP at 8​N8N per token on Phi-4-mini (N=3.84×109N=3.84\times 10^{9}) and roughly 1%1\% of the ∼360{\sim}360M-token main recovery run. The math-calibrated, web-recovered cell reaches the same range as the mw64 (math web 0.6 and 0.4) checkpoint under comparable protocols). The budget curve in Table 22 shows generation saturating near 3,2003{,}200 examples.

Seed replicates of the 2×22\times 2 design.

We repeat every cell of the 2×22\times 2 design on both models with two further recovery seeds (11 and 22) under the protocol of Table 20. On Llama-3.1-8B the sign is stable across recovery seeds. On Phi-4-mini every cell is similarly stable.

A.9 Held-out model and generation benchmarks

We verify our findings on interaction between calibration and recovery on the Qwen3-8B model in Table 23. We scored every 2×22\times 2 checkpoint and base on MBPP (3-shot), HumanEval+ (0-shot), and MATH-500 (4-shot, Minerva prompt). The three-task interaction is negative on all three models, with intervals excluding zero for Phi-4-mini and Qwen3-8B (Table 24). It is largest on HumanEval+, which reuses HumanEval’s prompts. The math-calibrated bases are much stronger than the web-calibrated ones, and on Llama-3.1-8B the no-recovery math base again beats both recovered cells. By benchmark (Table 24), the prompt-independent MBPP and MATH-500 contrast excludes zero only for Phi-4-mini. Llama’s MBPP contrast is positive, and MATH-500 shows no consistent effect.

A.10 MoE router precision

Router precision does not explain Qwen3-MoE’s strong 2-bit retention. Across two YAQA checkpoints, 2-bit routers remain essentially matched to fp16 routers (Table 29).

A.11 LoRA-based recovery

LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapters raise attainable generation accuracy for codebook recovery but change the trainable and stored parameterization, so we report them separately. HumanEval uses adapters folded into materialized weights. Across recovery datasets, QA stays stable, while the best generation task depends on recovery domain, with the same pattern on Llama (Table 30). The best folded Phi checkpoint reaches 34.834.8 IFEval prompt-strict accuracy.

Table 31 reports the remaining one-factor-at-a-time ablation axes. On Phi-4-mini, changing loss, temperature, logit support, or teacher precision leaves AvgQA nearly unchanged, while HumanEval varies more (Table 31).

A.12 Qwen3-8B

We evaluate Qwen3-8B (Yang et al., 2025), a third dense model, at 2 bits with math+web calibration. YAQA beats VPTQ on aggregate and generation metrics, and on all evaluated tasks except ARC-Easy (Table 32). Appendix A.9 also reports web and math YAQA bases with crossed recovery.

A.13 Separating sparsity from model scale with dense Qwen3-32B

As a size control for sparse Qwen3-30B-A3B, we quantize dense Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025) with 2-bit VPTQ on web Hessians. The dense model retains nearly all QA and completion-style generation (Table 33). HumanEval retention rises with total size within the Qwen3 family. Qwen3-MoE is highest, dense Qwen3-32B is between it and Qwen3-8B, and OLMoE is close to the smaller dense models. IFEval retention is similar for the two ∼30{\sim}30B models. We also evaluate another MoE, the OLMoE (Muennighoff et al., 2025) model both the 2-bit vector variants recover most of the bf16 AvgQA score (Table 34).

A.14 Additional analyses

Figures 6–7 summarize two cross-cutting trends from our 2-bit sweeps. Figures 8–10 and Table 37 add four supporting analyses. First, QA and next-word prediction survive 2-bit vector PTQ, while generation is fragile. Second, generation retention is model-dependent (Figure 9). Third, vector PTQ improves the nominal quality–rate trade-off. Fourth, the scalar 2-bit cliff holds across scalar PTQ methods and different models.

A.15 Generation under the 2-bit cliff

Figure 12 reproduces the main-paper generation teaser on Phi-4-mini. AvgGen is the mean of GSM8K and HumanEval. SpinQuant collapses by 3-bit and drops to zero at 2-bit, while a vector codebook (YAQA, mw64 base) restores part of the gap. Figure 1(b) adds recovery. Figures 13 and 14 extend Figure 1(b) to Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B. Each 2-bit method is plotted at its Table 4 score against training compute, with the 4-bit and 2-bit scalar ladder for reference. Vector PTQ (YAQA/VPTQ) matches or beats GSQ and BitDistiller at less compute. Dense Llama loses more generation at 2 bits, while Qwen3-MoE stays near its under-measured completion-prompt reference and retains more under the chat template.

A.16 Overthinking behavior at 2-bits: Additional Details

Figure 15 presents the effect of repetition penaty on accuracy and 4-gram lopp score at bf16 and 2-bit precisions.
